title: Data Classification
summary: Data classification is the practice of assigning every information asset a label that states how sensitive it is, and therefore how it must be handled. The label is not decoration: it drives which systems may store the data, who may read it, how it is encrypted, how long it is kept and how it is destroyed. Workable schemes use a small number of tiers, such as public, internal, confidential and restricted, and pair each tier with concrete handling rules, because a label with no rule attached changes nothing. The common mistake is classifying only documents while ignoring databases, logs, backups, chat exports and support tickets, which are where sensitive values usually leak from. Classification is the input to almost every other data protection control.

beginner.definition: Data classification means giving each piece of information a label that shows how sensitive it is. The label tells people and systems how the data must be stored, shared and destroyed. Most companies use a few simple levels, such as public, internal, confidential and restricted.
beginner.whyItMatters: You cannot protect everything in the same way, because that would be slow and expensive. Labels help you spend strong protection on the data that needs it most. Without labels, people guess, and guesses leak. A leaked customer list can cost money, trust and legal trouble. Clear labels also help you answer questions from auditors and regulators.
howItWorks: The company agrees on a small set of labels, such as public, internal, confidential and restricted.
Each label comes with clear rules for storage, sharing, copying and deletion.
A person or a tool looks at the data and chooses the right label.
The label is saved with the data, so people and systems can see it.
Tools enforce the rules, for example by blocking a restricted file from leaving.
The label is checked again when the data changes or the rules change.
beginner.example: Think of a shared flat with four flatmates. Everyone's post arrives in one hallway, so they agree on coloured envelopes. White is junk mail that anyone may open. Blue is household business, such as a utility bill. Yellow is personal post for one person. Red is a bank letter that must never be left in the hall. The colour is only useful because each one comes with a rule that everyone follows. If a flatmate writes red on an envelope and still leaves it on the table, the colour meant nothing. Classification works the same way, and the rule matters as much as the label.
takeaways: A label only helps when a clear handling rule is attached to it.
Classify data everywhere it lives, including logs, backups and support tickets.
Keep the number of levels small, so people really use them.

objectives: Explain what data classification means and why labels are used.
Describe how a handling rule turns a label into a real control.
Choose a suitable label for a given piece of data in a simple scenario.
Identify common places where unclassified sensitive data is overlooked.
Explain how classification supports other data protection controls.
